claim: Refractive index mismatches between media and sample cause spherical aberrations that often limit penetration depth and resolution in light microscopy.
source: In light microscopy, refractive index mismatches between media and sample cause spherical aberrations that often limit penetration depth and resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle of light microscopy.

claim: Optical clearing techniques are limited to fixed samples.
source: Optical clearing techniques can alleviate these mismatches, but they are so far limited to fixed samples.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a limitation of existing techniques.

claim: Iodixanol is a non-toxic medium supplement that allows refractive index matching in live specimens.
source: We present Iodixanol as a non-toxic medium supplement that allows refractive index matching in live specimens and thus substantially improves image quality in live-imaged primary cell cultures, planarians, zebrafish and human cerebral organoids.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Iodixanol supplementation substantially improves image quality in live-imaged primary cell cultures, planarians, zebrafish and human cerebral organoids.
source: We present Iodixanol as a non-toxic medium supplement that allows refractive index matching in live specimens and thus substantially improves image quality in live-imaged primary cell cultures, planarians, zebrafish and human cerebral organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figures 2-4.

claim: Refractive index mismatches between tissue and surrounding medium result in spherical aberrations that misalign the optical paths and ultimately distort and attenuate the microscopic image.
source: Refractive index mismatches between tissue and surrounding medium result in spherical aberrations that misalign the optical paths and ultimately distort and attenuate the microscopic image.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The effect of spherical aberrations increases with complexity and thickness of the specimen, making imaging in deep tissue layers difficult and technically demanding.
source: This effect increases with complexity and thickness of the specimen, making imaging in deep tissue layers difficult and technically demanding (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richardson and Lichtman, 2015.

claim: 2-photon microscopy greatly improves depth penetration by excitation with low scattering, near-infrared wavelengths.
source: 2-photon microscopy greatly improves depth penetration by excitation with low scattering, near-infrared wavelengths (Helmchen and Denk, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Helmchen and Denk, 2005.

claim: 2-photon microscopy cannot alleviate spherical aberration effects.
source: However, 2-photon microscopy cannot alleviate spherical aberration effects (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richardson and Lichtman, 2015.

claim: Adaptive optics microscopes can partially compensate for spherical aberrations.
source: These can be partially compensated by the recent introduction of adaptive optics microscopes (Booth, 2014), yet at the cost of reduced image acquisition rates and the need for intense excitation light.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Booth, 2014.

claim: Adaptive optics microscopes require reduced image acquisition rates and the need for intense excitation light.
source: These can be partially compensated by the recent introduction of adaptive optics microscopes (Booth, 2014), yet at the cost of reduced image acquisition rates and the need for intense excitation light.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of adaptive optics microscopy, supported by citation.

claim: Recently developed optical clearing techniques can render tissues effectively transparent by equilibrating refractive index heterogeneity within biological samples.
source: Indeed, recently developed optical clearing techniques can render tissues effectively transparent by equilibrating refractive index heterogeneity within biological samples (Chung et al., 2013; Hama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2013 and Hama et al., 2015.

claim: Optical clearing protocols remain limited to fixed specimens due to their reliance on harsh mounting conditions and/or toxic chemicals.
source: Unfortunately, these protocols remain limited to fixed specimens due to their reliance on harsh mounting conditions and/or toxic chemicals (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richardson and Lichtman, 2015.

claim: Iodixanol was originally developed as an intravenous X-ray contrast agent.
source: The compound Iodixanol, which was originally developed as an intravenous X-ray contrast agent (Albrechtsson et al., 1992) and widely used in density gradient applications (Bettinger et al., 2002), appeared to have many of the desired properties.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Albrechtsson et al., 1992.

claim: Iodixanol is widely used in density gradient applications.
source: The compound Iodixanol, which was originally developed as an intravenous X-ray contrast agent (Albrechtsson et al., 1992) and widely used in density gradient applications (Bettinger et al., 2002), appeared to have many of the desired properties.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bettinger et al., 2002.

claim: Iodixanol is commercially available under the brand name OptiPrep(TM).
source: Commercially available under the brand name OptiPrep(TM), Iodixanol is optically clear and displays a high refractive index of 1.429 as a 60% stock solution, likely at least in parts due to its high density.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the commercial availability of Iodixanol.

claim: Iodixanol is optically clear.
source: Commercially available under the brand name OptiPrep(TM), Iodixanol is optically clear and displays a high refractive index of 1.429 as a 60% stock solution, likely at least in parts due to its high density.
evidence: This is stated as an observed property of Iodixanol.

claim: Iodixanol displays a high refractive index of 1.429 as a 60% stock solution.
source: Commercially available under the brand name OptiPrep(TM), Iodixanol is optically clear and displays a high refractive index of 1.429 as a 60% stock solution, likely at least in parts due to its high density.
evidence: This is a measured property of Iodixanol, as shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The high refractive index of Iodixanol is likely at least in parts due to its high density.
source: Commercially available under the brand name OptiPrep(TM), Iodixanol is optically clear and displays a high refractive index of 1.429 as a 60% stock solution, likely at least in parts due to its high density.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed high refractive index.

claim: The refractive index of Iodixanol (1.429) is close to the refractive index of FocusClear (RI 1.47).
source: This value is close to the refractive index of popular fixed tissue clearing solutions such as FocusClear (RI 1.47) or CLARITY (RI 1.45) (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015), and Iodixanol has in fact been used in such protocols (Ku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison based on cited values from Richardson and Lichtman, 2015.

claim: The refractive index of Iodixanol (1.429) is close to the refractive index of CLARITY (RI 1.45).
source: This value is close to the refractive index of popular fixed tissue clearing solutions such as FocusClear (RI 1.47) or CLARITY (RI 1.45) (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015), and Iodixanol has in fact been used in such protocols (Ku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison based on cited values from Richardson and Lichtman, 2015.

claim: Iodixanol has been used in fixed tissue clearing protocols.
source: This value is close to the refractive index of popular fixed tissue clearing solutions such as FocusClear (RI 1.47) or CLARITY (RI 1.45) (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015), and Iodixanol has in fact been used in such protocols (Ku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ku et al., 2016.

claim: Iodixanol is highly water-soluble.
source: As Iodixanol is highly water-soluble, simple dilution into aqueous solutions can be used to linearly tune the refractive index of the solutions between RI 1.333 – RI 1.429 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a property of Iodixanol and demonstrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Simple dilution of Iodixanol into aqueous solutions can be used to linearly tune the refractive index of the solutions between RI 1.333 – RI 1.429.
source: As Iodixanol is highly water-soluble, simple dilution into aqueous solutions can be used to linearly tune the refractive index of the solutions between RI 1.333 – RI 1.429 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1a.

claim: For water, PBS and culture media of aquatic model organisms, the medium only minimally affected the refractive index at a given Iodixanol concentration.
source: For water, PBS and culture media of aquatic model organisms, the medium only minimally affected the refractive index at a given Iodixanol concentration (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1a.

claim: The temperature dependent change in refractive index of Iodixanol solutions is minimal within physiologically relevant temperature ranges.
source: Further, we found the temperature dependent change in refractive index (Beysens and Calmettes, 1977) of Iodixanol solutions to be minimal within physiologically relevant temperature ranges (Figure 1b), allowing the use of the same medium at multiple temperatures.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1b.

claim: The minimal temperature dependence of Iodixanol's refractive index allows the use of the same medium at multiple temperatures.
source: Further, we found the temperature dependent change in refractive index (Beysens and Calmettes, 1977) of Iodixanol solutions to be minimal within physiologically relevant temperature ranges (Figure 1b), allowing the use of the same medium at multiple temperatures.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed minimal temperature dependence.

claim: Agarose polymerization was not prevented at any Iodixanol concentration.
source: Agarose polymerization was not prevented at any Iodixanol concentration and agarose concentrations in ranges used for specimen immobilization did not significantly affect the refractive index of Iodixanol solutions (Figure 1c), thus making Iodixanol compatible with agarose embedding protocols.
evidence: This is an experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Agarose concentrations in ranges used for specimen immobilization did not significantly affect the refractive index of Iodixanol solutions.
source: Agarose polymerization was not prevented at any Iodixanol concentration and agarose concentrations in ranges used for specimen immobilization did not significantly affect the refractive index of Iodixanol solutions (Figure 1c), thus making Iodixanol compatible with agarose embedding protocols.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1c.

claim: Iodixanol is compatible with agarose embedding protocols.
source: Agarose polymerization was not prevented at any Iodixanol concentration and agarose concentrations in ranges used for specimen immobilization did not significantly affect the refractive index of Iodixanol solutions (Figure 1c), thus making Iodixanol compatible with agarose embedding protocols.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations about agarose polymerization and refractive index.

claim: A spectral emission scan of Iodixanol solutions at the commonly used excitation wavelengths of 405, 488, 560 and 640 nm failed to reveal significant autoflorescence in comparison with PBS or highly diluted fluorescent beads as negative or positive controls, respectively.
source: A spectral emission scan of Iodixanol solutions at the commonly used excitation wavelengths of 405, 488, 560 and 640 nm failed to reveal significant autoflorescence in comparison with PBS or highly diluted fluorescent beads as negative or positive controls, respectively (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Iodixanol solutions have no significant pH buffering capabilities within the physiological relevant pH range of pH 4 – pH 9.
source: pH titration curves demonstrate that Iodixanol solutions have no significant pH buffering capabilities within the physiological relevant pH range of pH 4 – pH 9, especially in comparison with PBS as classical physiological buffer (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1e.

claim: Iodixanol is only a slightly stronger acid than water.
source: In fact, Iodixanol is only a slightly stronger acid than water (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1e.

claim: Many optical clearing agents, such as ScaleA2, have a high intrinsic osmolality that makes the reagent intrinsically live specimen incompatible.
source: Finally, many optical clearing agents, such as ScaleA2, have a high intrinsic osmolality that makes the reagent intrinsically live specimen incompatible (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ke et al., 2013.

claim: 60% OptiPrep stock solution displays an osmolality of 212 ± 2 mmol/kg.
source: 60% OptiPrep stock solution displays an osmolality of 212 ± 2 mmol/kg, which is below the typical 290–300 mmol/kg of vertebrate cell culture media (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a measured value reported in the text and shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The osmolality of 60% OptiPrep stock solution (212 ± 2 mmol/kg) is below the typical 290–300 mmol/kg of vertebrate cell culture media.
source: 60% OptiPrep stock solution displays an osmolality of 212 ± 2 mmol/kg, which is below the typical 290–300 mmol/kg of vertebrate cell culture media (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured osmolality values.

claim: There is a linear increase of media osmolality across a dilution series with increasing Iodixanol concentrations.
source: Further, we measured a linear increase of media osmolality across a dilution series with increasing Iodixanol concentrations (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1f.

claim: The contribution of Iodixanol to overall media osmolality can be offset by a corresponding decrease in media salt concentration (e.g., NaCl).
source: This means that the contribution of Iodixanol to overall media osmolality can be offset by a corresponding decrease in media salt concentration (e.g., NaCl).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed linear increase in osmolality with Iodixanol concentration.

claim: Tuning of the refractive index of the bead solution to that of the used silicon immersion oil (RI = 1.40) greatly improved both the lateral and axial image resolution compared to controls mounted in conventional aqueous media (RI = 1.33).
source: As expected, tuning of the refractive index of the bead solution to that of the used silicon immersion oil (RI = 1.40), greatly improved both the lateral and axial image resolution compared to controls mounted in conventional aqueous media (RI = 1.33; Figure 1g,h; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1g,h and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The physicochemical properties of Iodixanol are ideally suitable for refractive index tuning of live imaging media.
source: Overall, the physicochemical properties of Iodixanol are therefore ideally suitable for refractive index tuning of live imaging media.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the physicochemical characterization data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Quantitative measurements failed to detect any Iodixanol concentration dependent effects on HeLa cell proliferation or cell death up to three days after plating, even at the highest tested concentration of 30% Iodixanol.
source: Our quantitative measurements failed to detect any Iodixanol concentration dependent effects on HeLa cell proliferation or cell death up to three days after plating, even at the highest tested concentration of 30% Iodixanol (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A concentration of 30% Iodixanol (RI = 1.380) is higher than the optimal Iodixanol concentration required for HeLa cells.
source: Importantly, a concentration of 30% Iodixanol (RI = 1.380) is higher than the optimal Iodixanol concentration required for HeLa cells.
evidence: This is stated as context for the toxicity assessment.

claim: At 72 hr post fertilization, all embryos developing in Iodixanol displayed normal motility, muscle contractions and body pigmentation.
source: At 72 hr post fertilization, all embryos developing in Iodixanol displayed normal motility, muscle contractions and body pigmentation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from zebrafish embryo development studies.

claim: Survival rates and the head to tail length of zebrafish embryos developing in Iodixanol were indistinguishable from controls.
source: Further, we found survival rates and the head to tail length as measure of developmental growth to be indistinguishable from controls, indicating that Iodixanol exposure over three days of development neither overtly affected development nor survival of zebrafish embryos (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2b.

claim: Iodixanol exposure over three days of development neither overtly affected development nor survival of zebrafish embryos.
source: Further, we found survival rates and the head to tail length as measure of developmental growth to be indistinguishable from controls, indicating that Iodixanol exposure over three days of development neither overtly affected development nor survival of zebrafish embryos (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is inferred from the survival and growth measurements.

claim: After 3 weeks of continuous exposure to 50% w/v Iodixanol, planarian specimens were healthy, had regenerated morphologically normal heads and succeeded in restoring normal body plan proportions.
source: Remarkably, even after 3 weeks of continuous exposure to a high concentration of Iodixanol, the specimens were healthy, had regenerated morphologically normal heads and succeeded in restoring normal body plan proportions as quantified by length to width ratio and projected area in a manner indistinguishable from controls (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2c.

claim: Planarians exposed to Iodixanol restored normal body plan proportions as quantified by length to width ratio and projected area in a manner indistinguishable from controls.
source: Remarkably, even after 3 weeks of continuous exposure to a high concentration of Iodixanol, the specimens were healthy, had regenerated morphologically normal heads and succeeded in restoring normal body plan proportions as quantified by length to width ratio and projected area in a manner indistinguishable from controls (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2c.

claim: Iodixanol supplementation minimally impacts survival and growth of cell cultures, embryonic development or tissue turn-over and regeneration in intact animals.
source: Collectively, these results establish that Iodixanol supplementation minimally impacts survival and growth of cell cultures, embryonic development or tissue turn-over and regeneration in intact animals, thus largely alleviating sample toxicity concerns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the toxicity assessment data in Figure 2.

claim: The refractive index of silicone oil (RI = 1.406) closely matches typical live specimens.
source: The refractive index of silicone oil, RI = 1.406 closely matches typical live specimens and its introduction has afforded a substantial improvement in live imaging quality (York et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation to York et al., 2012.

claim: The introduction of silicone oil immersion objectives has afforded a substantial improvement in live imaging quality.
source: The refractive index of silicone oil, RI = 1.406 closely matches typical live specimens and its introduction has afforded a substantial improvement in live imaging quality (York et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to York et al., 2012.

claim: In unsupplemented mounting media, the structure of nuclear chromatin was indiscernible in cells located 'behind' the first layer along the z-axis in primary zebrafish cell clusters.
source: In unsupplemented mounting media, the structure of nuclear chromatin was indiscernible in cells located 'behind' the first layer along the z-axis.
evidence: This is an observation from imaging experiments shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Tuning the mounting media RI to 1.362 reduced the degradation of image resolution for cells behind the first layer in primary zebrafish cell clusters.
source: Tuning the mounting media RI to 1.362 reduced the degradation of image resolution for such cells, demonstrating improvements in high resolution imaging of multi-layered cell culture applications (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Human cerebral organoids appear opaque due to the optical density of neuronal tissues.
source: Human cerebral organoids appear opaque due to the optical density of neuronal tissues (Figure 3b) (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, supported by citation to Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014.

claim: Conventional single photon microscopy cannot penetrate significantly beyond 20 µm depth in human cerebral organoids.
source: Consequently, conventional single photon microscopy cannot penetrate significantly beyond 20 µm depth (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3b.

claim: By mounting organoids in Iodixanol supplemented culture media (RI = 1.363), penetration depth was doubled to ~40 µm as a consequence of improved signal to noise ratios at depth.
source: By mounting organoids (67 days aged) in Iodixanol supplemented culture media (RI = 1.363), we doubled the penetration depth to ~40 µm as a consequence of improved signal to noise ratios at depth (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3b.

claim: Iodixanol supplementation improves depth penetration in organoid imaging.
source: Iodixanol supplementation thus improves depth penetration in organoid imaging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the organoid imaging data.

claim: The segmentation and tracking of cells beyond 100 µm in depth is a challenge in zebrafish embryos mounted in culture media (RI = 1.333).
source: Zebrafish embryos are a popular vertebrate development model system because of their optical transparency (Vascotto et al., 1997), yet the segmentation and tracking of cells beyond 100 µm in depth is still a challenge in embryos mounted in culture media (RI = 1.333, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge, supported by citation and demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RI tuning of the embedding media to RI 1.363 improved lateral resolution (792 ± 28 nm) compared to specimens mounted in regular media (918 ± 50 nm) at a distance of 150 µm from the coverslip in zebrafish embryos.
source: The quantification of lateral point spread functions between controls and embryos mounted in media tuned to a refractive index of RI 1.363 revealed an improvement of lateral resolution (792 ± 28 nm) compared to specimens mounted in regular media (918 ± 50 nm) at a distance of 150 µm from the coverslip (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4a.

claim: The resolution benefit of refractive index tuning increases with the distance of the object plane to the coverslip.
source: We found that the resolution benefit of refractive index tuning increases with the distance of the object plane to the coverslip (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 1), as expected from the increasing impact of spherical aberrations with increasing distance to the objective.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4a and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The increasing resolution benefit with distance is expected from the increasing impact of spherical aberrations with increasing distance to the objective.
source: We found that the resolution benefit of refractive index tuning increases with the distance of the object plane to the coverslip (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 1), as expected from the increasing impact of spherical aberrations with increasing distance to the objective.
evidence: This is an inference based on optical principles.

claim: RI tuning of the embedding media to RI 1.363 allowed segmentation of nuclei up to 300 µm in depth in zebrafish embryos.
source: Overall, RI tuning of the embedding media to RI 1.363 allowed segmentation of nuclei up to 300 µm in depth, thus demonstrating a substantial improvement of deep tissue imaging in developing zebrafish embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RI tuning demonstrates a substantial improvement of deep tissue imaging in developing zebrafish embryos.
source: Overall, RI tuning of the embedding media to RI 1.363 allowed segmentation of nuclei up to 300 µm in depth, thus demonstrating a substantial improvement of deep tissue imaging in developing zebrafish embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the zebrafish imaging data.

claim: Live imaging of planarian regeneration has so far not been possible.
source: Although these animals are widely studied as models of whole body regeneration, live imaging of planarian regeneration has so far not been possible.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current methods.

claim: Even unpigmented planarian species like Dendrocoelum lacteum are optically highly opaque.
source: Even unpigmented species like Dendrocoelum lacteum (Liu et al., 2013) are optically highly opaque, such that live imaging is largely restricted to the outermost cell layer (the epithelium; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, supported by citation to Liu et al., 2013 and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Live imaging of unpigmented planarians is largely restricted to the outermost cell layer (the epithelium).
source: Even unpigmented species like Dendrocoelum lacteum (Liu et al., 2013) are optically highly opaque, such that live imaging is largely restricted to the outermost cell layer (the epithelium; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4b.

claim: By tuning the refractive index of the embedding medium to RI 1.412, the opaque appearance of planarians was partially compensated and signal detection and overall signal to noise ratio in deeper cell layers were significantly improved.
source: By tuning the refractive index of the embedding medium to RI 1.412, we could partially compensate the opaque appearance of the specimen and significantly improve both signal detection and the overall signal to noise ratio in deeper cell layers (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4b.

claim: Iodixanol supplementation brings within reach the live-imaging of cell dynamics during planarian regeneration.
source: Together with the lack of overt effects on regeneration (Figure 2c), Iodixanol supplementation therefore brings within reach the live-imaging of cell dynamics during planarian regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the planarian imaging and toxicity data.

claim: Iodixanol supplementation is a simple, versatile and effective method for refractive index tuning in live imaging applications.
source: Overall, our results establish Iodixanol supplementation as a simple, versatile and effective method for refractive index tuning in live imaging applications.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented.

claim: The reduction of spherical aberrations between sample and mounting media by refractive index tuning provides substantial improvements in achievable imaging depth in planaria, zebrafish and human organoids.
source: We show that the reduction of spherical aberrations between sample and mounting media by refractive index tuning provides substantial improvements in achievable imaging depth in planaria, zebrafish and human organoids, as well as improved spatial resolution in cell culture applications.
evidence: This is a summary of the imaging improvements demonstrated in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Refractive index tuning with Iodixanol provides improved spatial resolution in cell culture applications.
source: We show that the reduction of spherical aberrations between sample and mounting media by refractive index tuning provides substantial improvements in achievable imaging depth in planaria, zebrafish and human organoids, as well as improved spatial resolution in cell culture applications.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3a for primary zebrafish cell cultures.

claim: Refractive index tuning with Iodixanol enables alignment of an important aspect of the optical axis in live specimens that could so far only be compensated in fixed specimens.
source: Refractive index tuning with Iodixanol therefore enables alignment of an important aspect of the optical axis in live specimens that could so far only be compensated in fixed specimens.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the significance of the method.

claim: Iodixanol supplementation cannot correct for refractive index differences within the specimen, such as between neighboring cells or between organelles and surrounding cytoplasm.
source: What Iodixanol supplementation cannot correct for are refractive index differences within the specimen, such as between neighboring cells or between organelles and surrounding cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the method.

claim: Refractive index differences within specimens are likely responsible for the fact that planarians and organoids appear optically opaque despite lacking pigmentation.
source: Such effects are likely responsible for the fact that planarians and organoids appear optically opaque despite lacking pigmentation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed opacity.

claim: Iodixanol cannot achieve the in-toto RI matching of fixed tissue protocols.
source: Even though Iodixanol can therefore not achieve the in-toto RI matching of fixed tissue protocols (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015), our results nevertheless demonstrate substantial imaging improvements even in the case of opaque specimens.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation compared to fixed tissue methods.

claim: Despite not achieving in-toto RI matching, Iodixanol demonstrates substantial imaging improvements even in the case of opaque specimens.
source: Even though Iodixanol can therefore not achieve the in-toto RI matching of fixed tissue protocols (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015), our results nevertheless demonstrate substantial imaging improvements even in the case of opaque specimens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data on opaque specimens like planarians and organoids.

claim: Refractive index tuning by Iodixanol supplementation represents a broadly useful addition to the tool kit of live-imaging applications, from cells to tissues and organisms.
source: Overall, we expect that refractive index tuning by Iodixanol supplementation represents a broadly useful addition to the tool kit of live-imaging applications, all the way from cells to tissues and organisms.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the expected utility of the method.

claim: Refractive indexes were measured at 20°C unless otherwise indicated.
source: Refractive indexes were measured at 20°C unless otherwise indicated.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Measurements of the refractive index were performed on a Rudolph Research Automatic Refractometer J457 at a wavelength of 589.3 nm.
source: Measurements of the refractive index were performed on a Rudolph Research Automatic Refractometer J457 at a wavelength of 589.3 nm.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Each refractive index measurement was performed as a technical triplicate.
source: Each measurement was performed as a technical triplicate and refractive indexes were measured at 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 50% and 60% final Iodixanol content.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Osmolality measurements were performed with a Wesco Vapro Osmometer as technical triplicates.
source: Osmolality measurements were performed with a Wesco Vapro Osmometer as technical triplicates.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: HeLa 'Kyoto' cells stably expressing H2B-mCherry were obtained from the Ellenberg group at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory Heidelberg.
source: HeLa 'Kyoto' cells stably expressing H2B-mCherry were described previously (Neumann et al., 2010) and obtained from the Ellenberg group at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory Heidelberg.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about cell line source.

claim: HeLa 'Kyoto' cells are not included in the Register of Misidentified Cell Lines v 8.0 curated by the International Cell Line Authentication Committee.
source: HeLa 'Kyoto' cells are not included in the Register of Misidentified Cell Lines v 8.0 curated by the International Cell Line Authentication Committee (Capes-Davis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as authentication information, supported by citation.

claim: The HeLa cell line was authenticated using Multiplex Cell Authentication by Multiplexion.
source: The cell line was authenticated using Multiplex Cell Authentication by Multiplexion (Heidelberg, Germany) as described (Castro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about cell line authentication, supported by citation.

claim: Mycoplasma tests with negative results for contamination were performed using the VenorGeM mycoplasma detection kit.
source: Mycoplasma tests with negative results for contamination were performed using the VenorGeM mycoplasma detection kit (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat No. MP0025).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about quality control.

claim: Dendrocoelum lacteum were cultured in planarian water at 13°C and were fed weekly with calf liver paste.
source: Dendrocoelum lacteum were cultured in planarian water at 13°C and were fed weekly with calf liver paste.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about animal husbandry.

claim: Prior imaging experiments, planarians were starved for 2 weeks.
source: Prior imaging experiments animals were starved for 2 weeks.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about experimental preparation.

claim: Human cerebral organoids were generated from human iPSC line SC102A-1.
source: Human cerebral organoids were generated from human iPSC line SC102A-1 (System Biosciences) and cultured according to previously published protocols with minor modification (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014 and Camp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about organoid generation, supported by citations.

claim: The culture media for organoids was replaced with an 18% Iodixanol/media v/v solution 24 hr prior imaging to match the refractive index of the tissue.
source: The culture media was replaced with an 18% Iodixanol/media v/v solution 24 hr prior imaging to match the refractive index of the tissue.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about sample preparation.

claim: The experiments performed with live samples did not require ethical approval according to German law.
source: The experiments performed with live samples did not require ethical approval according to German law.
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory compliance.
